clue: Sensory or visual warning sensation that may precede a seizure or migraine
rationale: The nurse asks about this prodromal symptom when taking a seizure or headache history.

clue: Drooping of the upper eyelid, seen in oculomotor nerve palsy or myasthenia gravis
rationale: The nurse notes this cranial nerve finding when performing a focused neurological exam.

clue: Loss of coordinated, voluntary muscle movement, often from cerebellar dysfunction
rationale: The nurse assesses gait and finger-to-nose testing to detect this sign of cerebellar involvement.

clue: Involuntary, rhythmic shaking movement of a body part
rationale: The nurse documents the type and timing of this movement, since it can point toward Parkinson's disease or withdrawal.

clue: Abnormal constriction of the pupil
rationale: The nurse checks pupil size along with reactivity when monitoring for opioid toxicity or brainstem injury.

clue: False sensation of spinning or movement, often from vestibular dysfunction
rationale: The nurse differentiates this from lightheadedness when a patient reports dizziness.

clue: Impaired ability to produce or understand language, commonly seen after a stroke
rationale: The nurse screens for this deficit early, since it affects how a patient can report pain or distress.

clue: Sudden, uncontrolled electrical disturbance in the brain causing altered movement or awareness
rationale: The nurse times and describes this event carefully, since the pattern guides the medical workup.

clue: Inability to perform a learned, purposeful motor task despite intact strength and sensation
rationale: The nurse distinguishes this from weakness when a stroke patient struggles to use a utensil correctly.

clue: In a state of deep, prolonged unconsciousness with no purposeful response to stimuli
rationale: The nurse uses the Glasgow Coma Scale to track a patient in this state and detect any change in level of consciousness.

clue: Localized collection of clotted blood outside a blood vessel
rationale: The nurse monitors a head injury for an expanding one of these, a sign of ongoing intracranial bleeding.

clue: Increased resistance to passive movement of a limb throughout its range of motion
rationale: The nurse tests for this finding when assessing a patient for Parkinson's disease or meningeal irritation.

clue: Forcible tearing away of tissue from its normal attachment
rationale: The nurse manages this traumatic wound by controlling bleeding and preserving any separated tissue.

clue: Double vision
rationale: The nurse asks about this visual symptom when screening for cranial nerve or increased intracranial pressure changes.

clue: Abnormal dilation of the pupil
rationale: The nurse notes this pupil change as a possible sign of increased intracranial pressure or certain drug effects.

clue: Involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes
rationale: The nurse observes for this eye movement during a cranial nerve exam, since it can signal vestibular or cerebellar issues.

clue: Complete loss of voluntary muscle function in a body part
rationale: The nurse documents the exact distribution of this deficit, since it helps localize a spinal or neurological injury.

clue: Unequal pupil size between the two eyes, a possible sign of rising intracranial pressure
rationale: The nurse reports this pupil finding immediately, since it can signal a neurological emergency.

clue: Slurred or unclear speech caused by impaired control of the muscles used for speaking
rationale: The nurse distinguishes this from aphasia, since language comprehension stays intact even though speech is hard to understand.

clue: Life-threatening displacement of brain tissue caused by rising intracranial pressure
rationale: The nurse watches for late signs of this complication, including a fixed and dilated pupil, after a severe head injury.

clue: Mild traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head
rationale: The nurse educates patients on watching for worsening symptoms after this common head injury.

clue: Weakness affecting one side of the body
rationale: The nurse tests grip strength on both sides to detect this asymmetric finding after a stroke.

clue: Abnormal posturing with flexed arms and extended legs, indicating a brain lesion above the brainstem
rationale: The nurse scores this posturing on the Glasgow Coma Scale motor response when assessing a severe brain injury.

clue: Abnormal posturing with extended, rigid limbs, indicating brainstem injury and a worse prognosis than the flexed form
rationale: The nurse recognizes this posturing as a more ominous neurological sign than decorticate posturing.
